newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Steelmaker failure hits S.Korea after strikes.
newsitem.headline: Steelmaker failure hits S.Korea after strikes.

text.p: South Korea's second biggest steel maker said on Friday it would file for court protection from its creditors, dealing a new blow to an economy reeling from almost a month of strikes.

Hanbo Steel Corp, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate, defaulted on debt payments on Thursday. Analysts said its collapse could spark a chain reaction of corporate bankruptcies and threaten banks.
Hanbo said it planned to file a court petition on Monday that would allow it to freeze payments on total debt of almost five trillion won ($5.8 billion).

Seeking to avert a financial crisis, the central Bank of Korea said it would pump liquidity into the financial system to ease a credit squeeze caused by the Hanbo failure, one of the most spectacular in South Korean history.
It also said it would make available emergency funds to Hanbo's suppliers and subcontractors that would be devastated by any debt repayment freeze.

Hanbo's collapse was caused largely by plant expansion it could not afford and had no direct connection to work stoppages sparked by passage of a new labour law that makes it easier for companies to lay off workers.
Nevertheless, it has sent shivers through labour unions who believe companies suffering from an economic downturn will seek to trim costs with staff redundancies.
Bankruptcies are rare in South Korea, where the government supports ailing companies indirectly by forcing banks to extend loans that make no commercial sense.
Economists said that if by allowing Hanbo to flop, authorities were signalling they would no longer prop up loss-making firms, an industrial shakeout could be on the way.
"Hanbo's default may signal the beginning of a chain reaction of corporate failures," said Lee Hahn-ku, president of Daewoo Research Institute.
"It is a big shock to the financial community. It could spark unemployment," Lee said.

He added: "Bankruptcies in the industrial sector will hit the financial community, which has been hostage to the government's industrial policy of picking winners and providing unlimited amounts of loans."
Banks on Friday were trying to stitch together a rescue package for Hanbo.

A total of 45 banks and other financial institutions have lent money to the company. Korea First Bank has the largest exposure of 1.1 trillion won. Other major creditors are the Korea Development Bank, Chohung Bank and Korea Exchange Bank.

Kim Joon-il, an economist at the Korea Development Institute, said some banks could be so severely hurt that the failure could hasten widely anticipated mergers and acquisitions in the financial industry.
"No one will want to take over Hanbo unless banks or the government write off much of the debt," said Lee of Daewoo.
Analaysts said the crisis as Hanbo Steel would have a domino effect on the group's other 21 subsidiaries because of cross-investments and cross-loan guarantees.

Banks said they planned to ask Pohang Iron and Steel Co, the country's largest steel maker, to complete expansion of Hanbo's mill in the southern city of Tangjin. The mill has so far cost 4.96 trillion won and a further 750 billion won is needed.
Hanbo's default drove Seoul stocks lower in early trading on Friday, but the market rebounded on bargain-hunting and the main index ended fractionally higher at 679.56 points.
